title: Long-Term Acute
Care
hero.text: For clinically complex patients who need specialist medical care, intensive coordination and longer recovery - bridging the gap between intensive care and home.

overview: Some patients are past the immediate crisis but still too medically complex for a general ward or home. Long-term acute care at Cambridge Hospital provides intensive, specialist-led management for these clinically complex patients who need more time, closer oversight and carefully coordinated care to recover.

Here, high-dependency medicine is delivered in a calmer and more personal environment. Every patient is treated as an individual, with a coordinated team working around a single shared plan, allowing recovery to continue at a pace appropriate to the patient’s condition and needs.

blocks.text: Long-term acute care (LTAC) is for patients who remain seriously ill or medically fragile after the acute phase of their illness and who need hospital-level care for an extended period.

These are patients whose needs are too complex for a standard ward. They may require prolonged respiratory support, complex wound care, intensive medication management or coordination of several conditions at once.
LTAC provides the sustained specialist attention and coordinated care that a longer and more complex recovery demands.

topics.label: When Long-Term Acute Care Is Needed

blocks.text: Patients may benefit from long-term acute care when a serious illness, injury or complication leaves them stable enough to leave intensive care but still dependent on close medical management.

This may include patients recovering from prolonged critical illness, those undergoing ventilator weaning, patients with complex or non-healing wounds or patients managing multiple serious conditions at the same time.
The common thread is medical complexity that requires time and specialist expertise to manage, with care tailored to each patient’s condition, needs and progress.

topics.label: Beyond the ICU: A Place to Continue Recovery

blocks.text: For many complex patients, the intensive care unit should not be the end of the road.

Once the immediate emergency has passed, a medically stable patient can often continue their recovery in a specialised setting designed for longer stays, offering close clinical monitoring in a more comfortable and less intensive environment.
Moving to long-term acute care gives patients more space and time to focus on recovery, while providing families with the reassurance of continued specialist care and support throughout the process.
Complex patients need close coordination across multiple areas of care.

At Cambridge Hospital, physicians lead an interdisciplinary team of specialist nurses, respiratory therapists, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, dietitians and pharmacists who work together around a shared care plan.

This coordinated approach ensures that each aspect of a complex patient’s care is carefully managed carefully and that the different elements of treatment work comprehensively towards the patient’s recovery.
Respiratory care is one of Cambridge Hospital’s core strengths.

Our teams manage patients on short and long-term mechanical ventilation, including those with a tracheostomy, and use a structured, protocol-based approach to weaning - gradually and safely reducing ventilator dependence where clinically appropriate so patients can breathe independently again where possible.
Where full independence from the ventilator isn’t possible, our focus remains on maintaining respiratory stability and supporting the patient’s comfort and quality of life.

topics.label: Complex Wounds, Nutrition and Multi-System Care

blocks.text: Long-term acute illness can involve several complex needs at the same time.
Our teams manage complex and slow-healing wounds, nutritional and feeding needs and the careful management of multiple medical conditions and medications.

By treating the whole patient rather than a single problem, we help reduce complications and establish the foundation for steady, lasting progress - supporting patients not only medically, but in achieving the greatest possible level of comfort, function and independence.
